claim: The Ethics committee of the Medical Faculty, University of Leipzig, Germany approved the study (protocol number 273/14-ff).
source: The Ethics committee of the Medical Faculty, University of Leipzig, Germany approved the study (protocol number 273/14-ff).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval documented in the manuscript.

claim: 33 participants were recruited using the database of the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences, Leipzig, Germany.
source: We recruited 33 participants using the database of the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences, Leipzig, Germany.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant recruitment in the methods section.

claim: Participants were right handed as assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: The participants were right handed (as assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory; Oldfield, 1971), native German-speakers, had a mean age and standard deviation (SD) of 24.9 ± 2.5 years, and included 23 females.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant characteristics with citation support.

claim: Participants had a mean age of 24.9 ± 2.5 years.
source: The participants were right handed (as assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory; Oldfield, 1971), native German-speakers, had a mean age and standard deviation (SD) of 24.9 ± 2.5 years, and included 23 females.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant demographics.

claim: 23 of the 33 participants were females.
source: The participants were right handed (as assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory; Oldfield, 1971), native German-speakers, had a mean age and standard deviation (SD) of 24.9 ± 2.5 years, and included 23 females.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant demographics.

claim: Participants were native German-speakers.
source: The participants were right handed (as assessed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory; Oldfield, 1971), native German-speakers, had a mean age and standard deviation (SD) of 24.9 ± 2.5 years, and included 23 females.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant characteristics.

claim: None of the participants reported a history of psychiatric or neurological disorders, hearing difficulties, or current use of psychoactive medications.
source: None of the participants reported a history of psychiatric or neurological disorders, hearing difficulties, or current use of psychoactive medications.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusion criteria.

claim: Normal hearing abilities were confirmed with pure tone audiometry (250 Hz to 8000 Hz) with a threshold equal to and below 25 dB.
source: Normal hearing abilities were confirmed with pure tone audiometry (250 Hz to 8000 Hz) with a threshold equal to and below 25 dB (Madsen Micromate 304, GN Otometrics, Denmark).
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant screening procedures.

claim: The role of sensory thalami for human cognition and perception remains unclear.
source: Sensory thalami are central sensory pathway stations for information processing. Their role for human cognition and perception, however, remains unclear.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Recent evidence suggests an involvement of the sensory thalami in speech recognition.
source: Recent evidence suggests an involvement of the sensory thalami in speech recognition.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing prior research.

claim: The auditory thalamus (medial geniculate body, MGB) response is modulated by speech recognition tasks.
source: In particular, the auditory thalamus (medial geniculate body, MGB) response is modulated by speech recognition tasks and the amount of this task-dependent modulation is associated with speech recognition abilities.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing prior findings.

claim: The amount of task-dependent modulation in the MGB is associated with speech recognition abilities.
source: In particular, the auditory thalamus (medial geniculate body, MGB) response is modulated by speech recognition tasks and the amount of this task-dependent modulation is associated with speech recognition abilities.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract summarizing prior findings.

claim: Ultra-high field 7T fMRI was used to identify the vMGB.
source: We used ultra-high field 7T fMRI to identify the vMGB, and found a significant positive correlation between the amount of task-dependent modulation and the speech recognition performance across participants within left vMGB, but not within the other MGB subsections.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract about the methods used.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the amount of task-dependent modulation and speech recognition performance across participants within left vMGB.
source: We used ultra-high field 7T fMRI to identify the vMGB, and found a significant positive correlation between the amount of task-dependent modulation and the speech recognition performance across participants within left vMGB, but not within the other MGB subsections.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the main finding in the abstract.

claim: There is no significant positive correlation between the amount of task-dependent modulation and speech recognition performance in other MGB subsections.
source: We used ultra-high field 7T fMRI to identify the vMGB, and found a significant positive correlation between the amount of task-dependent modulation and the speech recognition performance across participants within left vMGB, but not within the other MGB subsections.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a negative finding in the abstract.

claim: Modulation of thalamic driving input to the auditory cortex facilitates speech recognition.
source: These results imply that modulation of thalamic driving input to the auditory cortex facilitates speech recognition.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the results stated in the abstract.

claim: Human communication relies on fast and accurate decoding of speech.
source: Human communication relies on fast and accurate decoding of speech—the most important tool available to us for exchanging information.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the introduction based on general knowledge.

claim: Speech is the most important tool available to humans for exchanging information.
source: Human communication relies on fast and accurate decoding of speech—the most important tool available to us for exchanging information.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the introduction based on general knowledge.

claim: Understanding the neural decoding mechanisms for speech recognition is important for understanding human brain function.
source: Understanding the neural decoding mechanisms for speech recognition is important for understanding human brain function (Rauschecker and Scott, 2009), but also for understanding communication disorders such as developmental dyslexia (Galaburda et al., 1994; Müller-Axt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support.

claim: Understanding the neural decoding mechanisms for speech recognition is important for understanding communication disorders such as developmental dyslexia.
source: Understanding the neural decoding mechanisms for speech recognition is important for understanding human brain function (Rauschecker and Scott, 2009), but also for understanding communication disorders such as developmental dyslexia (Galaburda et al., 1994; Müller-Axt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support.

claim: Since the early findings of Wernicke (1874) neuroscientific models of speech recognition have mainly focused on cerebral cortex mechanisms.
source: Since the early findings of Wernicke (1874) neuroscientific models of speech recognition have mainly focused on cerebral cortex mechanisms (Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Friederici and Gierhan, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the history of the field.

claim: A full understanding of speech recognition mechanisms might need to take the subcortical sensory pathways—particularly the sensory thalami—into account.
source: Yet, more recently it has been suggested that a full understanding of speech recognition mechanisms might need to take the subcortical sensory pathways—particularly the sensory thalami—into account (von Kriegstein et al., 2008a; Díaz et al., 2012; Díaz et al., 2018; Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Chandrasekaran et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about recent theoretical developments.

claim: The classic view that the sensory thalamus is a passive relay station has been by-and-large abandoned over the last two decades.
source: The classic view, that the sensory thalamus is a passive relay station has been by-and-large abandoned over the last two decades.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the evolution of scientific understanding.

claim: There are strong corticofugal projections to the sensory thalamus.
source: First of all, it is well known that there are strong corticofugal projections to the sensory thalamus (Sherman and Guillery, 2006; Winer and Prieto, 2001; Lee and Sherman, 2012; Lee and Winer, 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical connectivity.

claim: Sensory thalamus responses are modulated by attention.
source: Furthermore, experimental evidence in humans and other mammals in the visual as well as the auditory modality has shown that sensory thalamus responses are modulated by attention (Saalmann and Kastner, 2011), percept (Haynes et al., 2005), context (Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; McAlonan et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2002), and task (Díaz et al., 2012; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about functional properties.

claim: Sensory thalamus responses are modulated by percept.
source: Furthermore, experimental evidence in humans and other mammals in the visual as well as the auditory modality has shown that sensory thalamus responses are modulated by attention (Saalmann and Kastner, 2011), percept (Haynes et al., 2005), context (Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; McAlonan et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2002), and task (Díaz et al., 2012; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about functional properties.

claim: Sensory thalamus responses are modulated by context.
source: Furthermore, experimental evidence in humans and other mammals in the visual as well as the auditory modality has shown that sensory thalamus responses are modulated by attention (Saalmann and Kastner, 2011), percept (Haynes et al., 2005), context (Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; McAlonan et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2002), and task (Díaz et al., 2012; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about functional properties.

claim: Sensory thalamus responses are modulated by task.
source: Furthermore, experimental evidence in humans and other mammals in the visual as well as the auditory modality has shown that sensory thalamus responses are modulated by attention (Saalmann and Kastner, 2011), percept (Haynes et al., 2005), context (Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; McAlonan et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2002), and task (Díaz et al., 2012; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about functional properties.

claim: The sensory thalamus has become accepted as a structure that is modulated by cognitive demands and is more involved in active information regulation.
source: Based on these findings, the sensory thalamus has become accepted as a structure that is modulated by cognitive demands and is more involved in active information regulation (Saalmann and Kastner, 2011; Haynes et al., 2005; Antunes and Malmierca, 2011; McAlonan et al., 2008; O'Connor et al., 2002; Díaz et al., 2012; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b), for a different take see Camarillo et al. (2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the current consensus view.

claim: Previous studies showed a task-dependent modulation in the auditory sensory thalamus for auditory speech recognition.
source: In the case of speech, previous studies showed a task-dependent modulation in the auditory sensory thalamus for auditory speech recognition, (MGB; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2012) as well as a task-dependent modulation in the visual sensory thalamus for visual speech recognition (LGN; Díaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about prior findings.

claim: Previous studies showed a task-dependent modulation in the visual sensory thalamus for visual speech recognition.
source: In the case of speech, previous studies showed a task-dependent modulation in the auditory sensory thalamus for auditory speech recognition, (MGB; von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2012) as well as a task-dependent modulation in the visual sensory thalamus for visual speech recognition (LGN; Díaz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about prior findings.

claim: Bilateral MGB showed significantly higher responses to an auditory speech recognition task than to control tasks, independent of attentional load or task-difficulty.
source: In the MGB there were two findings: First, bilateral MGB showed significantly higher responses to an auditory speech recognition task than to control tasks, independent of attentional load or task-difficulty (von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about prior findings.

claim: The performance level in the auditory speech recognition task was significantly correlated with the task-dependent modulation in the MGB of the left hemisphere across participants.
source: Second, the performance level in the auditory speech recognition task was significantly correlated with the task-dependent modulation in the MGB of the left hemisphere across participants (von Kriegstein et al., 2008b).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about prior findings.

claim: The MGB consists of three divisions.
source: The MGB consists of three divisions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about anatomical organization.

claim: Only the ventral MGB (vMGB) can be considered first-order sensory thalamus.
source: Only the ventral MGB (vMGB) can be considered first-order sensory thalamus (Malmierca et al., 2015 [review], Winer et al., 2005 [review]), as vMGB receives driving inputs from sources that relay information from the sensory periphery and projects this information to the cerebral cortex (Sherman and Guillery, 1998).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical classification.

claim: vMGB receives driving inputs from sources that relay information from the sensory periphery and projects this information to the cerebral cortex.
source: Only the ventral MGB (vMGB) can be considered first-order sensory thalamus (Malmierca et al., 2015 [review], Winer et al., 2005 [review]), as vMGB receives driving inputs from sources that relay information from the sensory periphery and projects this information to the cerebral cortex (Sherman and Guillery, 1998).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical connectivity.

claim: Ventral MGB receives modulatory input from cerebral cortex.
source: Ventral MGB also receives modulatory input from cerebral cortex (Sherman and Guillery, 1998).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical connectivity.

claim: The dorsal (dMGB) and medial MGB (mMGB) do not show major projections to primary auditory cortices.
source: In contrast, the other two MGB divisions, the dorsal (dMGB) and medial MGB (mMGB), do not show major projections to primary auditory cortices (Vasquez-Lopez et al., 2017; Anderson et al., 2007; de la Mothe et al., 2006), and are not considered to be part of the first order (i.e., lemniscal) auditory pathway (Anderson et al., 2007; Anderson et al., 2009; Calford, 1983; Cruikshank et al., 2001; Gonzalez-Lima and Cada, 1994; Hackett et al., 1998; Morest, 1964; Winer et al., 1999); although see Anderson and Linden (2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical connectivity.

claim: The dorsal (dMGB) and medial MGB (mMGB) are not considered to be part of the first order (i.e., lemniscal) auditory pathway.
source: In contrast, the other two MGB divisions, the dorsal (dMGB) and medial MGB (mMGB), do not show major projections to primary auditory cortices (Vasquez-Lopez et al., 2017; Anderson et al., 2007; de la Mothe et al., 2006), and are not considered to be part of the first order (i.e., lemniscal) auditory pathway (Anderson et al., 2007; Anderson et al., 2009; Calford, 1983; Cruikshank et al., 2001; Gonzalez-Lima and Cada, 1994; Hackett et al., 1998; Morest, 1964; Winer et al., 1999); although see Anderson and Linden (2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical classification.

claim: The human MGB is approximately 5 × 4 × 5 mm in size.
source: Due to the relatively small size of human MGB (ca. 5 × 4 × 5 mm, Winer, 1984) and the spatial limitations of the non-invasive imaging techniques used in previous studies (von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2012), it was so far not possible to differentiate in which of the three major MGB divisions there is behaviorally relevant task-dependent modulation for speech.
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about anatomical dimensions.

claim: It was so far not possible to differentiate in which of the three major MGB divisions there is behaviorally relevant task-dependent modulation for speech due to the small size of human MGB and spatial limitations of non-invasive imaging techniques.
source: Due to the relatively small size of human MGB (ca. 5 × 4 × 5 mm, Winer, 1984) and the spatial limitations of the non-invasive imaging techniques used in previous studies (von Kriegstein et al., 2008b; Díaz et al., 2012), it was so far not possible to differentiate in which of the three major MGB divisions there is behaviorally relevant task-dependent modulation for speech.
evidence: This is a direct statement about limitations of prior research.

claim: Ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 7 Tesla enables high spatial resolution measurements.
source: Here we, therefore, used ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 7 Tesla, enabling high spatial resolution measurements (Duyn, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the capabilities of the imaging method.

claim: The vMGB has a strong tonotopic organization.
source: The vMGB has a strong tonotopic organization (Calford, 1983; Rodrigues-Dagaeff et al., 1989; Anderson et al., 2007) while the other two MGB subsections have only a weak tonotopic organization (i.e., broadly tuned neurons; Anderson and Linden, 2011; Calford, 1983; Bartlett and Wang, 2011; Rodrigues-Dagaeff et al., 1989; Ohga et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about functional organization.

claim: The other two MGB subsections have only a weak tonotopic organization (i.e., broadly tuned neurons).
source: The vMGB has a strong tonotopic organization (Calford, 1983; Rodrigues-Dagaeff et al., 1989; Anderson et al., 2007) while the other two MGB subsections have only a weak tonotopic organization (i.e., broadly tuned neurons; Anderson and Linden, 2011; Calford, 1983; Bartlett and Wang, 2011; Rodrigues-Dagaeff et al., 1989; Ohga et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about functional organization.

claim: The vMGB was distinguished based on its tonotopic organization as well as its topographic (i.e., ventral) location.
source: We planned to distinguish the vMGB based on its tonotopic organization as well as its topographic (i.e., ventral) location.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodological approach.

claim: Three fMRI paradigms were employed: an MGB localizer, a tonotopy localizer, and the speech experiment.
source: We employed three fMRI paradigms—an MGB localizer, a tonotopy localizer, and the speech experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: In the MGB localizer and the tonotopy localizer, participants listened to natural sounds (human voices, animal cries, tool sounds).
source: In the MGB localizer and the tonotopy localizer (Figure 1A), participants listened to natural sounds (human voices, animal cries, tool sounds) (Moerel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: The MGB localizer served to identify the left and right MGB.
source: The MGB localizer served to identify the left and right MGB.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the purpose of the localizer.

claim: The tonotopic maps resulting from the tonotopy localizer were used to localize the left and right vMGB.
source: The tonotopic maps resulting from the tonotopy localizer were used to localize the left and right vMGB.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the purpose of the tonotopy localizer.

claim: In the speech experiment, participants listened to blocks of auditory syllables (e.g.,/aba/).
source: In the speech experiment (Figure 1B and C), participants listened to blocks of auditory syllables (e.g.,/aba/), and performed either a speech or a speaker task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: In the speech task, participants reported via button press whether the current syllable was different from the previous one (1-back task).
source: In the speech task, participants reported via button press whether the current syllable was different from the previous one (1-back task).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental task.

claim: In the speaker task, participants reported via button press whether the current speaker was different from the previous one.
source: In the speaker task, participants reported via button press whether the current speaker was different from the previous one.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental task.

claim: Two tonotopic gradients were found within the MGB in the group analysis.
source: Similar as in Moerel et al. (2015), we found two tonotopic gradients within the MGB in the group analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of the tonotopy analysis.

claim: One high frequency region in the middle of the MGB was flanked by gradually lower frequency components dorsally and ventrally.
source: On visual inspection, one high frequency region in the middle of the MGB was flanked by gradually lower frequency components dorsally and ventrally (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the tonotopic organization with reference to figures.

claim: The two tonotopic gradients run dorso-lateral to ventro-medial.
source: The two gradients run dorso-lateral to ventro-medial.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the orientation of the tonotopic gradients.

claim: The mean gradient distributions across individuals for the left MGB had maxima at 130° and 300°.
source: The analysis of the mean gradient distributions across individuals (Figure 3, black line with standard error of the mean in gray) for the left MGB had maxima at 130° and 300° (dashed red lines, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the quantitative analysis of gradient directions with reference to figures.

claim: In the right MGB the mean across individual distributions had maxima at 130° and 310°.
source: In the right MGB the mean across individual distributions had maxima at 130° and 310°.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the quantitative analysis of gradient directions.

claim: Gradient one was located ventrally and slightly medial compared to gradient 2 in the left MGB.
source: For the left MGB, gradient one was located ventrally and slightly medial compared to gradient 2, which was situated more anterior, dorsal, and lateral.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the spatial location of the gradients.

claim: Gradient 2 was situated more anterior, dorsal, and lateral in the left MGB.
source: For the left MGB, gradient one was located ventrally and slightly medial compared to gradient 2, which was situated more anterior, dorsal, and lateral.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the spatial location of the gradients.

claim: For the right MGB, gradient one was more ventral and medial compared to gradient 2.
source: For the right MGB we found similar locations: gradient one was more ventral and medial compared to gradient 2.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the spatial location of the gradients.

claim: Gradient one represents the vMGB based on the tonotopy and its ventral location.
source: Based on the tonotopy and its ventral location (Morel et al., 1997; Bartlett and Wang, 2011) we considered gradient one to represent the vMGB (Moerel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the interpretation of the gradients.

claim: Participants scored a mean hit rate in the speech task of 0.872 with 97% highest posterior density (HPD) interval [0.828, 0.915].
source: Participants scored a mean hit rate in the speech task of 0.872 with 97% highest posterior density (HPD) interval [0.828, 0.915], and a mean hit rate in the speaker task of 0.760 with a 97% HPD interval [0.706, 0.810] (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about behavioral results with reference to figures.

claim: Participants scored a mean hit rate in the speaker task of 0.760 with a 97% HPD interval [0.706, 0.810].
source: Participants scored a mean hit rate in the speech task of 0.872 with 97% highest posterior density (HPD) interval [0.828, 0.915], and a mean hit rate in the speaker task of 0.760 with a 97% HPD interval [0.706, 0.810] (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about behavioral results with reference to figures.

claim: The mean hit-rate was 0.112 higher in the speech task than in the speaker task with 97% HPD interval [0.760, 0.150].
source: The mean hit-rate was 0.112 higher in the speech task than in the speaker task with 97% HPD interval [0.760, 0.150].
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison of behavioral results.

claim: There was no evidence for higher BOLD response in the speech task in comparison to the speaker task (speech vs speaker contrast) in vMGB.
source: Unexpectedly, there was no evidence for higher BOLD response in the speech task in comparison to the speaker task (speech vs speaker contrast) in vMGB.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a null finding in the fMRI results.

claim: The correlation coefficient r=0.46 (R²=0.21) is considered to represent a large effect.
source: The correlation coefficient r=0.46 (R²=0.21) is considered to represent a large effect (Cohen, 1988 p. 80), explaining 21% of the variance of either variable when linearly associated with the variance in the other.
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the interpretation of the effect size.

claim: The correlation explains 21% of the variance of either variable when linearly associated with the variance in the other.
source: The correlation coefficient r=0.46 (R²=0.21) is considered to represent a large effect (Cohen, 1988 p. 80), explaining 21% of the variance of either variable when linearly associated with the variance in the other.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the correlation.

claim: The meta-analysis yielded an overall large effect size of d = 0.85 [0.06, 1.65], p=0.036.
source: The meta-analysis yielded an overall large effect size of d = 0.85 [0.06, 1.65], p=0.036 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the meta-analysis results with reference to a figure.

claim: Four of the five experiments had a positive medium to large effect and only the current study had a very small insignificant negative effect.
source: The analysis showed that four of the five experiments had a positive medium to large effect and only the current study had a very small insignificant negative effect.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the meta-analysis results.

claim: The confidence intervals from the current study do not overlap with those of the other studies.
source: The confidence intervals from the current study also do not overlap with those of the other studies.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison of confidence intervals.

claim: The result of the speech task vs control task contrast of the current study is different from the other studies compared in the meta-analysis.
source: In terms of equivalence testing (Schuirmann, 1987), this means that the result of the speech task vs control task contrast of the current study is different from the other studies compared here.
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the interpretation of the meta-analysis.

claim: Performance in the speech and the speaker tasks was significantly correlated (r = 0.77, p<0.001).
source: Performance in the speech and the speaker tasks was significantly correlated (r = 0.77, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the correlation between behavioral measures.

claim: There was no difference in the correlation between the contrast speech vs speaker task and the speech recognition scores and the correlation of the contrast speech vs speaker with the speaker recognition score (z = −0.717, p=0.474).
source: Accordingly, there was no difference in the correlation between the contrast speech vs speaker task and the speech recognition scores and the correlation of the contrast speech vs speaker with the speaker recognition score (z = −0.717, p=0.474).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison of correlations.

claim: There was no correlation (speech vs speaker task correlated with speech recognition performance across participants) in the left MGB–gradient 2.
source: There was no correlation (speech vs speaker task correlated with speech recognition performance across participants) in the left MGB–gradient 2 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a null finding in the exploratory analysis.

claim: The comparison of the two correlations (i.e., for left vMGB and left MGB-gradient 2) showed that they are significantly different (z = 4.466, p<0.0001).
source: The comparison of the two correlations (i.e., for left vMGB and left MGB-gradient 2) showed that they are significantly different (z = 4.466, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison of correlations.

claim: The behaviorally relevant task-dependent modulation for speech is specific to the left vMGB.
source: Thus, this is a first indication that the behaviorally relevant task-dependent modulation for speech is specific to the left vMGB.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the exploratory analysis.

claim: There were no significant effects in any other regions outside the vMGB in exploratory analyses.
source: In exploratory analyses we tested the main effect of task (speech vs speaker contrast) and the correlation of the speech vs speaker contrast with behavioral performance in the speech task in several areas outside the vMGB, for which we did not have an a priori hypothesis. There were no significant effects in any other regions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about null findings in exploratory analyses.

claim: It is the left auditory first-order sensory thalamus – the left ventral subdivision of the MGB (vMGB) – that is modulated during speech recognition.
source: Using ultra-high field fMRI we showed that it is the left auditory first-order sensory thalamus – the left ventral subdivision of the MGB (vMGB) – that is modulated during speech recognition.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the main finding in the discussion.

claim: The vMGB is the primary sensory pathway nucleus of the auditory thalamus and transmits input to the cerebral cortex.
source: The vMGB is the primary sensory pathway nucleus of the auditory thalamus and transmits input to the cerebral cortex (Winer, 1984; Anderson et al., 2007; Bartlett et al., 2011; Bordi and LeDoux, 1994; Calford, 1983; Moerel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the functional role of vMGB.

claim: When decoding speech, higher order cortical areas modify representations of the sensory input in the primary sensory thalamus and such modification is relevant for speech recognition abilities.
source: The present results imply that, when decoding speech, higher order cortical areas modify representations of the sensory input in the primary sensory thalamus and that such modification is relevant for speech recognition abilities.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of the results.

claim: Speech recognition might only be fully understood if dynamic cortico-thalamic interactions are taken into account.
source: These results are a further indication that speech recognition might only be fully understood if dynamic cortico-thalamic interactions are taken into account (Klostermann et al., 2013; von Kriegstein et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is a direct statement with citation support about the theoretical implications.

claim: Although we found no significant main effect in the vMGB (nor in any other subregion of the MGB), the correlation between the task-dependent modulation and behavioral performance was, as hypothesized, significant within the left vMGB.
source: The results are based on the test of two equally weighted hypotheses: a main effect and a correlation. Although we found no significant main effect in the vMGB (nor in any other subregion of the MGB), the correlation between the task-dependent modulation and behavioral performance was, as hypothesized, significant within the left vMGB.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the pattern of results.

claim: The tonotopic organization of the vMGB has been observed in many species with the use of invasive techniques.
source: The tonotopic organization of the vMGB has been observed in many species with the use of invasive techniques (Winer, 1984; Anderson et al., 2007; Bartlett et al., 2011; Bordi and LeDoux, 1994; Calford, 1983) and non-invasively in six human participants using ultra-high field fMRI (Moerel et al., 2015).
